title: Love and grief
hookLine: grief is love with nowhere to go, as many say

lines: A COAT STILL BY THE DOOR.
GRIEF AND LOVE, SIDE BY SIDE.
cards: A coat still hangs by the door, months later. Nobody wears it. Nobody can move it either.

A phone holds a voicemail that never gets deleted. A recipe card sits in a drawer in handwriting that won't come again. Small things, and they can stop a person cold in the middle of an ordinary afternoon.
People sometimes put it this way: grief is love with nowhere to go. In the Gospel of John, there's a scene where grief and love show up side by side, in the same breath.

teach.b: First, the scene. Jesus has a friend named Lazarus, in the village of Bethany, with his sisters Martha and Mary. Lazarus falls sick and dies before Jesus arrives.
When Jesus comes, Mary falls at his feet weeping, and the people with her are weeping too. Jesus asks where they have laid him. Then comes a verse of two words, in the King James text: "Jesus wept."
Second, what the onlookers see. They don't say, look how sad he is.
The text has them say, "Behold how he loved him!" Standing by a grave, they read his tears as love: the grief was the shape the love took. Third, the surprise.
In John's story, Jesus is about to call Lazarus out of the tomb. The ending is close.
And still he weeps. Some Christians see in it that hope doesn't cancel grief; the loss is real, and it's honored with tears. Fourth, the line from the hook.
It's a saying, not a scripture, but it fits the scene.
Love that used to have a phone number, a chair at the table, a person to reach now has nowhere to land, so it comes out as tears, or as a coat that can't be moved.

Seen this way, grief isn't a sign that something went wrong with you. It's evidence of what was there. Different traditions hold death and what follows it in very different ways, and this lesson won't choose among them.
But on any path, the tears can be read the way the people at Bethany read them.

how: Traditions mark grief in their own ways: Jewish mourners sit shiva, Christians hold funerals and remember the dead in prayer, Muslims pray the funeral prayer and visit the family, Hindus and Sikhs each hold their own rites and recitations for the departed, and many Buddhists chant and make offerings in their name.

o: the village where Jesus wept for his friend Lazarus
the town where Jesus was born to Mary and Joseph
the garden where Jesus prayed the night of his arrest

games.q: who's who at Bethany — tap the pairs.
p: wept, though the ending was close

s: in John's story, Jesus doesn't weep because he knows Lazarus will live
the people at the tomb read his tears as love
"grief is love with nowhere to go" is a line from scripture
it's a saying people use, not a verse, though it fits the scene.

games.q: you're standing with the crowd at Bethany, and you see Jesus weeping at his friend's grave. what do the people say?
games.why: the text has them say, "behold how he loved him!" his tears are read as love. some others there ask whether he couldn't have kept his friend from dying.

practice: If it feels right today, bring to mind one grief, a person, a place, a pet, a time of life, a friendship that ended; if nothing comes, that's fine too, just sit with the breath.

If something does come, let it be there without fixing it, and quietly say beside it, not instead of it: it was love. If tears come, let them; if you pray, you can hold this one in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Bethany. The village where Lazarus died, and where the onlookers watched Jesus weep and said, behold how he loved him. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: he wept, shed tears, the verb in John 11:35.

carryVoice: Your line: it was love. A loss that still catches you off guard is love, remembering. Day eight hundred seventy-three.
